questions.q: Which capability distinguishes an L7 load balancer from a pure L4 one?
options: Routing requests based on URL path or HTTP headers
Distributing TCP connections across backend servers
Terminating client TCP connections
Running periodic health checks against registered backends
questions.explanation: Only L7 parses the application protocol, so only it can route on paths, headers, or cookies. Connection distribution and health checks are things both layers do.

questions.q: When is least-connections a better choice than round-robin?
options: When all requests take an identical, predictable amount of time
When backends must be chosen by client IP
When request durations vary widely between requests
When session stickiness is strictly required
questions.explanation: With variable request durations, open-connection count is a live proxy for how busy a backend is, so least-connections adapts. Round-robin is fine only when work per request is uniform.

questions.q: What is the purpose of an active health check from a load balancer?
options: To measure client-perceived latency from the edge
To balance load according to CPU usage
To encrypt all traffic flowing between the balancer and backends
To probe backends and stop routing to failing ones
questions.explanation: Active health checks periodically probe each backend so unhealthy instances are removed from rotation before users hit them. They are about availability, not encryption or CPU-based weighting.

questions.q: What problem do sticky sessions solve?
options: Uneven CPU utilization across heterogeneous backend servers
Keeping a user's requests on the server holding their session state
Rotating TLS certificates without downtime
Slow DNS propagation between regions
questions.explanation: Stickiness pins a client to the backend that holds its in-memory session so state stays reachable. It trades even load distribution for that affinity.

questions.q: What is the main benefit of consistent hashing for backend selection?
options: Encrypting the hash of every request
Guaranteeing perfectly equal load distribution across every backend server
Eliminating the need for health checks
Minimizing remapping when servers are added or removed
questions.explanation: Consistent hashing moves only the keys owned by the changed node instead of reshuffling everything as modulo hashing does. Distribution is approximately even, not perfect, which is why virtual nodes exist.

questions.q: A balancer that decides using only IP addresses and TCP/UDP ports operates at which layer?
options: Layer 7
Layer 4
Layer 2
Layer 5
questions.explanation: Ports belong to the transport layer, so IP-and-port routing is Layer 4. Layer 7 would require reading the application payload such as HTTP.

questions.q: Why do L4 load balancers generally push more throughput than L7 proxies?
options: They skip parsing application payloads and simply forward packets or connections
They cache HTTP responses at the edge
They compress all forwarded traffic
They use UDP instead of TCP for internal forwarding
questions.explanation: Forwarding packets without parsing or buffering HTTP costs far less CPU per byte. L7 proxies pay for the visibility that enables content-based routing.

questions.q: In weighted round-robin, a server weighted 3 versus others at 1 will?
options: Get three retry attempts per request
Receive one-third of the total traffic
Receive about three times as many requests
Be probed three times during every health-check cycle
questions.explanation: Weights set the relative share of requests, so weight 3 draws roughly triple what a weight-1 peer gets. The actual fraction depends on how many other servers exist.

questions.q: A backend passes TCP health checks but its application is deadlocked and returns nothing. What helps?
options: Lower the TCP health-check interval so failures are detected much sooner
Use HTTP health checks that verify a real application response
Add several more backends to the pool
Switch the balancer from L7 to L4 mode
questions.explanation: A TCP handshake only proves the socket is listening, so an application-level check that requires a valid HTTP response is needed. Probing a broken check more often just fails faster at nothing.

questions.q: Sticky sessions are enabled and one backend dies. What typically happens to its users?
options: Nothing happens, because sessions replicate automatically between all backends through the balancer itself
Their requests hang until the server returns
The balancer restores their sessions from its own memory
They get rerouted and lose in-memory session state unless it's stored externally
questions.explanation: The balancer reassigns those clients to healthy backends, but local session data dies with the instance. Externalizing state to Redis or a database is the standard fix.

questions.q: Under plain round-robin one backend becomes five times slower but stays healthy. The effect?
options: The balancer automatically detects the slowdown and shifts new traffic away from it immediately
Requests to it fail fast with 503 responses
In-flight requests pile up on it while it still receives an equal share
Health checks eject it within one cycle
questions.explanation: Round-robin is oblivious to latency and load, so the slow node keeps its equal share and queues grow. Least-connections or latency-aware policies would shift traffic away.

questions.q: A single load balancer is a single point of failure. The standard remedy?
options: Run redundant balancer pairs with failover via a VIP, DNS, or anycast
Move the balancing logic into the database tier
Use one much larger balancer instance
Have every client library retry failed requests until the single balancer restarts itself
questions.explanation: Redundant balancers sharing a floating VIP, DNS failover, or anycast remove the single point of failure. A bigger single instance is still one instance.

questions.q: All employees behind one corporate NAT hash to the same backend under source-IP affinity. Consequence?
options: Perfect load spread, since IP hashing is uniform
TLS handshakes fail for those specific clients
That backend becomes a hot spot carrying the whole office's traffic
The NAT gateway automatically rewrites their requests to reach other backends instead
questions.explanation: IP hashing is uniform over distinct IPs, but NAT collapses many users into one source address, so they all land on one backend. That concentration creates a hot spot.

questions.q: What is a key limitation of DNS-based (GSLB) load balancing?
options: Cached DNS answers make traffic shifts slow and unreliable to propagate
It cannot return multiple IP addresses
It only works for UDP-based services
It requires deep L7 inspection of every single DNS query passing through
questions.explanation: Resolvers and clients cache records, often ignoring TTLs, so draining a region by DNS takes minutes or longer. DNS can absolutely return multiple A records.

questions.q: Connection draining (deregistration delay) exists so that?
options: New TLS sessions warm up gradually across the backend pool
In-flight requests finish before a backend is removed
Health checks get extra time to pass during deploys
The balancer can compress idle connections safely
questions.explanation: Draining stops sending new requests while letting existing ones complete, so deploys and scale-downs do not sever active work. Without it, users see reset connections.

questions.q: You need TLS termination, path-based routing to microservices, and gRPC awareness. Which fits?
options: A pure L4 passthrough network load balancer with simple TCP health checks
Round-robin DNS records pointing at the services
An IP-hash router operating at L3
An L7 proxy such as Envoy or an application load balancer
questions.explanation: Path routing and gRPC or HTTP/2 awareness require parsing the application protocol, which is exactly what an L7 proxy does. L4 passthrough cannot see paths at all.

questions.q: Why does 'power of two choices' beat naive random backend assignment?
options: Sampling two servers and picking the less-loaded one sharply cuts imbalance
Two balancers double the achievable throughput
It halves the total health-checking overhead
Two independent hash functions eliminate assignment collisions entirely across the pool
questions.explanation: Comparing just two random candidates reduces maximum load from logarithmic to log-log growth, a large win for almost no extra cost. It is about smoothing load, not raw throughput.

questions.q: Backends slow down, health checks fail, the pool shrinks, and survivors get more load — a spiral. Best mitigation?
options: Tighten health-check thresholds even further
Retry every failed request more aggressively until the backend pool finally stabilizes
Disable health checking permanently across the fleet
Use circuit breaking, retry budgets, and gradual ejection instead
questions.explanation: Circuit breakers, retry budgets, and capped outlier ejection shed load and stop the feedback loop. Tighter thresholds or aggressive retries add load and accelerate the collapse.

questions.q: Consistent hashing over three equal servers; one dies. Ideally, what fraction of keys must remap?
options: All of the keys in the ring
About half of the keys
Roughly one-third — only the keys the dead server owned
None; requests simply queue up until the dead server eventually returns
questions.explanation: Only the failed node's arc of the ring moves, so about 1/N of keys, here one-third, are reassigned to its successors. Modulo hashing would instead remap nearly everything.

questions.q: Long-lived gRPC (HTTP/2) connections through an L4 balancer end up imbalanced. Why?
options: The HTTP/2 spec requires sticky sessions
The balancer spreads connections, not the many multiplexed requests inside each one
gRPC clients disable health checking by default
The balancer downgrades HTTP/2 streams to HTTP/1.1 connections unevenly across backends
questions.explanation: L4 balances at connection setup, but HTTP/2 multiplexes thousands of pinned requests over one persistent connection. The fix is L7 request-level balancing or client-side load balancing.
